grounding: It shows a new employee seeing a senior backdate a safety form, told it is normal, and letting the wish to fit in quiet his unease.

passage:
In her second week at the milk collection centre outside Anand, Vidya watched the queue of cans stretch past the neem tree. The truck to the dairy left at eight sharp.
Raghav Bhaiya, who had worked there eleven years, tested the first few cans properly, then began writing the same figure for the rest without dipping the meter.
'Bhaiya, those aren't tested.'
'Same farmers every day, same milk,' he said, not looking up. 'If we test every can, the truck leaves without us. This is how it works here.'
Vidya nodded. It did make sense, sort of. Nobody else in the shed seemed bothered. The farmer at the counter smiled at her.
Still, as the truck pulled out, she kept thinking about the untested cans, and said nothing.

qa.q: What time did the truck to the dairy leave?
qa.a: The truck left at eight sharp.

qa.q: Why does Vidya stay silent even though she keeps thinking about the untested cans?
qa.a: She is new, Raghav Bhaiya is senior, and no one else seems bothered, so wanting to fit in outweighs her unease.

qa.q: What turning point is open to Vidya at this early stage?
qa.a: She could ask Raghav Bhaiya or the centre in-charge how to test faster, so the truck is met without skipping, before the shortcut becomes normal for her.

qa.q: How might the farmers be affected if untested cans become routine?
qa.a: Farmers who bring good milk could be paid the same as anyone else, and their trust depends on fair testing they cannot see.

grounding: It shows a new worker watching a senior skip tests to meet the truck, told it is how things work, and staying quiet despite unease.

passage:
Three weeks into her job as a quality technician at a food factory outside Johannesburg, Lindiwe watched Lars, the senior technician, fill in last Tuesday's fridge temperature log. It was Friday.
"We missed a couple of checks," he said, writing neat numbers into each box. "Auditor comes Monday. Everyone does this. It's how things work here."
The numbers looked perfectly normal. Lindiwe felt a small cold knot in her stomach. Had the fridge actually been fine on Tuesday? Nobody knew.
Lars handed her the clipboard. "Can you initial the Wednesday ones? Saves time."
She hesitated. Everyone in the lab liked Lars. She was new, on probation, and didn't want to be the difficult one before her first audit.
"Sure," she said, and initialled three boxes. It took ten seconds. On the drive home the unease sat quietly in the passenger seat. She made a note to check the fridge herself first thing Monday, then told herself the rest was nothing.

qa.q: When is the auditor coming?
qa.a: Auditor comes Monday.

qa.q: What was Lindiwe feeling when Lars handed her the clipboard?
qa.a: She felt uneasy, with a cold knot in her stomach, but the pressure to fit in as a new hire on probation outweighed it.

qa.q: What could Lindiwe have done instead of initialling?
qa.a: Politely said she could only sign checks she did herself, and asked how missed checks are normally reported.

qa.q: How might Lars see the backdating?
qa.a: Lars seems to see it as routine and harmless, a normal way of saving time before audits.

grounding: A new employee watches a colleague backdate a log, is told it's how things work, and joins in as the pressure to fit in outweighs her unease.

passage:
In the staffroom of the government school in Guwahati, Sabina, three months into her first teaching job, watched Bidisha fill in the science practical register. Twenty-eight students, twenty-eight neat marks out of twenty. The practical had been cancelled twice because the lab had no chemicals.
"The inspection's next week," Bidisha said without looking up. "We can't show zero practicals. Everyone does it this way. Just give them a fair average."
Sabina's stomach tightened. Some of those students had never touched a test tube.
"Your section's register is on the shelf," Bidisha added kindly. "Do it now, or the head will be upset."
Sabina looked around. Two other teachers were doing the same, chatting about a wedding. Nobody seemed troubled. She was the new one; she wanted them to like her.
She picked up her pen and started filling in marks. Each number felt like a very small lie. She told herself it was only for one term.

qa.q: Why had the practical been cancelled?
qa.a: The lab had no chemicals.

qa.q: What was Sabina feeling as she filled in the marks?
qa.a: She felt uneasy and guilty, each number a small lie, but the pressure to fit in as the new teacher won.

qa.q: What could Sabina have done instead?
qa.a: Talked to the head about the missing chemicals and recorded the practical honestly as not held, asking how to report it.

qa.q: How does Bidisha seem to see the register?
qa.a: Bidisha sees it as a harmless routine that protects the school at inspection, and is kind in showing Sabina.

grounding: A new teacher sees colleagues fill in marks for a practical never held, is told everyone does it, and joins in despite her unease.

passage:
Hey Madhav,
Quick question, and be honest. Something happened at site today and I can't stop thinking about it.
We were supposed to wait for the full-strength concrete test before pouring the next slab. Our supervisor said the client wants the floor done before Diwali, so he wrote "test passed" on the form using an early result and a projected number. He said, "Everyone does it. The mix is fine. It's how the industry works."
He asked me to sign as site engineer. I'm four months in. The whole team was watching. I signed.
Probably the concrete is fine. Probably nothing will happen. But I felt sick in the site office afterwards and didn't eat lunch. So tomorrow I'm asking the lab to rush the real test, and I'll make sure the props under that slab stay until the result comes, whatever he says.
Is this how it's going to be? Tell me I'm overthinking it.
Jaya

qa.q: What did the supervisor write on the form?
qa.a: Test passed.

qa.q: What did Jaya feel after signing?
qa.a: Jaya felt sick and uneasy, unable to eat lunch, though the pressure to fit in had won in the moment.

qa.q: What protective step does Jaya plan, and why does it matter?
qa.a: Asking the lab to rush the real test and keeping the slab propped until then, because a safety shortcut on concrete could hurt people.

qa.q: How might Madhav feel reading this email?
qa.a: Madhav would likely feel concerned and want to tell Jaya the unease is right to take seriously.

grounding: A new engineer signs off a shortcut on a test after being told it's how things work, then feels uneasy and takes a protective step.

passage: Deepak turned his chair around and told Shreya, his new flatmate, about his first week. "So I'm Deepak, the fresher in quality at the pump factory. On Thursday a batch was due to ship at six. The pressure test is meant to run fifteen minutes per pump. My senior ran each one for five and signed the sheet for fifteen. I said, 'Sir, isn't it fifteen?' And he laughed. 'Everybody knows five is enough. Target is target. That's how things work here, boss.' The others nodded like I'd asked why the sky is blue. I felt this little knot in my stomach. But then I thought, he's been there nine years, who am I? And honestly, I wanted them to like me. So by the evening I was holding the stopwatch too. Five minutes. I don't know. It's probably fine, right?"

qa.q: How long is the pressure test meant to run per pump?
qa.a: It is meant to run fifteen minutes per pump.

qa.q: What does the little knot in Deepak's stomach suggest?
qa.a: It suggests Deepak felt uneasy and guilty about the shortened test, but the wish to be liked and fit in was stronger.

qa.q: What turning point is available to Deepak at this first step?
qa.a: Deepak could quietly ask the quality manager or check the written procedure about the test time, before this becomes his normal too.

qa.q: How might Shreya see Deepak's question at the end?
qa.a: Shreya may sense Deepak is looking for reassurance and feel unsure whether to comfort him or tell him honestly that it doesn't sound fine.

grounding: Shows a new employee seeing a colleague cut a test to meet a target, being told it is normal, and going along despite unease to fit in.
